plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two identical cubic crystal lattices drawn side by side in perspective. Each is a three-by-three-by-three array of small red spheres standing for atoms, joined by thin black lines tracing the cube edges and the rows between nearest neighbors, so the block reads as open and transparent. In the left lattice, a translucent teal plane lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the middle sheet of atoms, appearing darker where it sits behind the front layer of spheres and paler where it emerges near the top face. In the right lattice, the highlighted plane is tilted instead, slicing diagonally from the lower left of the cube toward the upper right and intersecting a different set of spheres, its shading again splitting between a darker interior portion and a lighter one near the top. Holding the lattice fixed while changing only the orientation of the shaded plane makes that orientation the single variable in view. The pair conveys that one crystal holds many families of parallel atomic planes at differing angles and spacings, each able to produce its own X-ray diffraction.

elements: 27 red atom spheres arranged in a 3x3x3 simple-cubic grid (indices 0,1,2 on each axis)
thin black line segments joining every pair of nearest-neighbor atoms along x, y, and z (the cube edges and interior rows)
outer cube silhouette formed by the edge lines so the block reads as open/transparent
one translucent teal atomic plane (double-sided quad) clipped to the cube bounding box
plane orientation controlled by Miller indices (h,k,l): face-parallel (100) vertical sheet, diagonal (110) sheet, steeper diagonal (111) sheet
plane offset index n selecting which parallel member of the family is highlighted (passes through a chosen sheet/diagonal row of atoms)
spacing label 'd = a / sqrt(h^2+k^2+l^2)' shown near the plane, updating with the family
small axis triad or x/y/z labels at the cube corner for orientation reference

interactions.label: Plane family (hkl)
interactions.teaches: One fixed crystal contains many families of parallel atomic planes at different angles; rotating the highlighted plane through the same red-sphere lattice shows each family cuts a different set of atoms

interactions.label: Plane index n
interactions.teaches: Stepping n moves the translucent sheet to the next parallel plane in the chosen family, so successive sheets light up different rows of atoms and the d-spacing label ties orientation + spacing to the Bragg diffraction condition

demo_steps.title: Face-parallel (100) planes
demo_steps.narration: With (hkl)=(100) the teal sheet is parallel to a cube face and passes through the middle column of atoms (n=1). These are the widely spaced, face-on planes.

demo_steps.title: Step to the next (100) plane
demo_steps.narration: Increase n to 2: the sheet jumps one lattice constant to the next parallel face-plane, highlighting the next row of spheres. Spacing d = a.

demo_steps.title: Diagonal (110) family
demo_steps.narration: Switch the family to (110). The same lattice now shows a plane tilted 45° cutting diagonally through a different set of atoms; its spacing shrinks to d = a/√2.

demo_steps.title: Body-diagonal (111) family
demo_steps.narration: Switch to (111): an even steeper diagonal sheet with the tightest spacing d = a/√3, demonstrating that more steeply inclined families are more closely packed.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Lattice constant a = 1 world unit; atoms at integer coords (i,j,k) with i,j,k in {0,1,2}, so the cube spans 0..2 on each axis (~2 units side). Atom spheres: SphereGeometry radius ~0.09, color #cc3333 with slight specular highlight. Bond lines: thin black (#111111) LineSegments between nearest neighbors only (|Δ|=1 along one axis). Teal plane color #5fb3a8, opacity ~0.45, DoubleSide, depthWrite false so spheres behind it stay visible (darker-through effect). Plane defined by Miller indices: normal = normalize(h,k,l), plane equation h*x+k*y+l*z = n, positioned at offset n/|n_vec| along the normal and clipped to the [0,2]^3 bounding box (build a large PlaneGeometry and intersect, or compute the convex polygon of the box-plane intersection). Family mapping: (100)->(1,0,0), (110)->(1,1,0), (111)->(1,1,1). d-spacing label value = 1/sqrt(h^2+k^2+l^2) (in units of a). Valid n that intersect atoms: (100): 0,1,2; (110): 0..4; (111): 0..6 — clamp slider n to the family's max so an empty plane is never shown. Default view matches the left source image (face-parallel middle sheet).
interactionPlan.notes: Build the lattice once and keep it static; only the teal plane mesh and the d-spacing text update on interaction. Recompute the clipped plane polygon whenever planeFamily or planeIndex changes (hide the plane if n is out of the family's intersecting range). Render the spacing label as an HTML overlay or sprite anchored near the plane centroid. Use a subtle ambient + directional light so the red spheres read as 3D balls like the source. Keep orbit disabled (not requested) so the orientation variable stays unambiguous, matching the textbook's fixed-viewpoint comparison.

authoredContext:
Although the figure depicts a crystal as a two-dimensional array of scattering centers for simplicity, real crystals are structures in three dimensions. Scattering can occur simultaneously from different families of planes at different orientations and spacing patterns known as called Bragg planes, as shown in the figure. The resulting interference pattern can be quite complex.

Because of the regularity that makes a crystal structure, one crystal can have many families of planes within its geometry, each one giving rise to X-ray diffraction.

Figure shows two crystal lattices, with atoms shown as small circles, connected to each other by lines. In the first lattice, flat planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In the second, slanted planes formed in the lattice are highlighted. In each case, the planes are seen as a combination of different atoms in the same lattice.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure shows two identical cubic crystal lattices drawn side by side in perspective. Each is a three-by-three-by-three array of small red spheres standing for atoms, joined by thin black lines tracing the cube edges and the rows between nearest neighbors, so the block reads as open and transparent. In the left lattice, a translucent teal plane lies parallel to one pair of cube faces and passes through the middle sheet of atoms, appearing darker where it sits behind the front layer of spheres and paler where it emerges near the top face. In the right lattice, the highlighted plane is tilted instead, slicing diagonally from the lower left of the cube toward the upper right and intersecting a different set of spheres, its shading again splitting between a darker interior portion and a lighter one near the top. Holding the lattice fixed while changing only the orientation of the shaded plane makes that orientation the single variable in view. The pair conveys that one crystal holds many families of parallel atomic planes at differing angles and spacings, each able to produce its own X-ray diffraction.
